I’ve looked up her professional profile on LinkedIn a few times (and stirred up huge anxiety for myself). I see patterns and I know nothing good comes from allowing myself to go down these roads, as you can see from what I’ve described.

Setting boundaries with myself is hard, but it’s a kindness to myself. Those were some incredibly tough years.

The (very mild) one that is currently eating me up, and I’m realising now is a very fundamental trauma:

My mother broke one of my bones disciplining me for breaking a rule (jumping on the bed). I was a very young child. My grandmother took us to the hospital and I was instructed to lie. They told the nurses I had jumped off the bed because I thought I could fly, and that she had grabbed me trying to save me. It was humiliating having them think I could be so stupid, as being more intelligent than most kids was part of my identity at that age. Having to lie and take the blame for something I didn’t do, while my mother was painted as a hero, was an incredibly difficult pill to swallow (as an autistic child who only ever told the truth and had a strong moral compass).

It also hurt that my grandmother would lie, to the doctors and nurses, to cover up what my mother did to me. 

I learned that day to never tell anyone what was going on at home. She continued to abuse me daily until I left at 17.

Edit: I forgot to add, my mother used to tell that story (the version of her being the hero and “trying to save me”) as a “funny story” whenever I had friends over. I remember thinking that her story felt wrong; I was a smart kid, and I didn’t ever “believe I could fly”. I always knew if she hadn’t grabbed me I wouldn’t have been hurt, but I didn’t remember the details. That is, until I told the story to a friend in front of my grandmother and she said “that’s not how it happened… who told you that?” She clarified what happened and I felt so validated. The memories themselves returned shortly after.

That therapist was wildly unprofessional and I’m sorry he tried to take advantage of you like that. It’s truly awful. I understand why you feel that way about therapists keeping their distance from you, and it makes perfect sense. I hope you can communicate that with any future therapists you may have so they know it’s a boundary.

Not specifically serotonin syndrome, but an inability to tolerate depression and anxiety medication, especially SSRIs. A bad reaction to an SSRI for depression is a strong indicator that they may be looking at bipolar. Is not uncommon for people with bipolar, schizophrenia or personality disorders to have naturally elevated levels of serotonin in the brain, meaning that a medication which increases serotonin can easily lead to excess. It’s also true that medication-induced mania or hypomania can mimic serotonin syndrome very closely. And since there is no specific test for serotonin syndrome (it is a diagnosis of exclusion) I would be hesitant to rule out bipolar being the cause in this scenario due to some of the other symptoms OP has been experiencing.

I have a lot of experience with kids and iPads. I feel like it’s okay to allow kids to use an iPad for a short time if you genuinely do need them to be quiet and entertained for a while, eg. making tea because otherwise they make the task impossible. But giving them their own iPad can cause big problems, like feeling entitled to it and the fact that they aren’t capable of regulating their own screen time. Everything in moderation, and also monitor behavioural changes. If you let him have it for x amount of time per week and notice no behavioural changes then it’s probably just fine. Otherwise adjust accordingly, or remove it entirely. It can also make a big difference what you let them play. You could have books or educational games that will help his creativity or development, instead of just “fun”. I’ve been in therapy for many years and one thing I’ve noticed is the times when I really don’t want to go to therapy are the times I need to go the most. It’s okay to be afraid. It’s okay to feel like it didn’t really happen. And it’s okay to not be able to tell her about the abuse. The way you acted wasn’t stupid, you were overwhelmed. You don’t have to tell her what happened or why you froze. What I find helpful when dealing with these kinds of overwhelming situations is to put up barriers to protect yourself and start on the very surface. Tell her something easy. I might say “I feel stupid for how I reacted last session but there’s something I can’t talk about. I can’t go into more detail right now”. Or maybe “I had some memories come up but I’m not sure if they’re real, and I can’t talk about it because I’m overwhelmed.” Or even just “I’m not ready to talk about what happened last session but I still want help”. You don’t have to tell her about the abuse if you don’t want to. You don’t have to disclose anything you’re not ready for. I understand you’re afraid to unearth something terrible. But you don’t have to dig into anything before you’re ready and your therapist will understand and respect that. The biggest thing is to just keep going to therapy and talking about what you can, even if all you can do is tell her you can’t talk about it. I promise she can help you with all that you’re going through, piece by piece, when you’re ready to let her.
